COPYRIGHT MANAGEMENT INFORMATION (17 U.S.C. § 1202) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS COPYRIGHT MANAGEMENT INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes 17 U.S.C. § 1202, the Digital Millennium Copyright Act section titled “Integrity of copyright management information,” which prohibits providing or distributing false copyright management information (“CMI”) and prohibits removing or altering CMI in the circumstances the statute specifies, together with the civil remedies for a violation set out in 17 U.S.C. § 1203 and the criminal penalties set out in 17 U.S.C. § 1204. It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes concerning Acme, Inc.'s A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. Section 1202 concerns the identifying information carried with a work — the information set out in a copyright notice, the title, the name of the author or copyright owner, terms and conditions for use, and identifying numbers or links referring to that information, including when such information travels with a digital file as metadata — rather than the creative content of the work itself. A claim under § 1202 is therefore a different claim from copyright infringement under 17 U.S.C. § 501: the statutory elements of § 1202 turn on the handling of CMI and on the actor's state of mind with respect to infringement, and the section is enforced through the separate civil action created by § 1203. This document is a general informational reference describing what the statute and the published decisions say; it is not a court filing, a demand letter, a compliance certification, or legal advice about whether any particular handling of A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. does or does not violate 17 U.S.C. § 1202.

HOW THIS INFORMATION SHEET RELATES TO THIS PROJECT'S OTHER COPYRIGHT DOCUMENTS
Section 1202 sits beside several other parts of Title 17 that this project covers in separate documents, and this Information Sheet does not restate them. 17 U.S.C. § 512, the notice-and-takedown safe harbor addressed by this project's DMCA Takedown Notice, DMCA Counter-Notification, and § 512(c) safe harbor documents, concerns an online service provider's liability for material stored or transmitted at a user's direction and the notice procedure for removing or restoring it. 17 U.S.C. § 1201, addressed by this project's DMCA Anti-Circumvention and Reverse-Engineering Exemptions Information Sheet, concerns circumventing technological measures that control access to a work and trafficking in circumvention tools; § 1201 and § 1202 are separate prohibitions that share the single civil-remedies section, § 1203, and the single criminal-penalties section, § 1204. Registration of a copyright claim with the U.S. Copyright Office, addressed by this project's copyright registration document, is a separate subject from the CMI conveyed with copies of a work. The attribution and integrity rights of visual artists under the federal Visual Artists Rights Act and the California Art Preservation Act, addressed by this project's documents on those statutes, are separate rights that attach to certain works of visual art and are not the subject of § 1202. This Information Sheet concerning A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. addresses §§ 1202–1204 only.

SECTION 1202(A): PROVIDING OR DISTRIBUTING FALSE COPYRIGHT MANAGEMENT INFORMATION
17 U.S.C. § 1202(a) prohibits two acts involving false CMI: providing copyright management information that is false (§ 1202(a)(1)), and distributing or importing for distribution copyright management information that is false (§ 1202(a)(2)). Both acts are governed by a single mental-state phrase placed at the front of the subsection: the person must act “knowingly and with the intent to induce, enable, facilitate, or conceal infringement.” Subsection (a) states that intent requirement in one form only; unlike subsection (b), which is addressed in a separate clause of this document, subsection (a) contains no alternative “reasonable grounds to know” standard for civil cases. A person injured by a violation of § 1202 may bring a civil action under 17 U.S.C. § 1203(a).

The Ninth Circuit decision cited elsewhere in this document (Stevens v. Corelogic) construes § 1202(b), not § 1202(a), and no case-law citation is offered here for subsection (a): CourtListener's public search index, the only case-law retrieval path available in this environment, is rate-limited and shared, and the research for this document budgeted its queries to the § 1202(b) decision rather than relying on unverified recollection of other holdings. This clause also does not address the limitations in § 1202(d) and § 1202(e) or the criminal provision in § 1204, each of which is described in a separate clause, and it does not state whether any particular labeling, credit, or watermark practice involving A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. is or is not false CMI. SECTION 1202(B): REMOVAL OR ALTERATION OF COPYRIGHT MANAGEMENT INFORMATION
17 U.S.C. § 1202(b) prohibits three acts, each only when done “without the authority of the copyright owner or the law”: intentionally removing or altering any CMI (§ 1202(b)(1)); distributing or importing for distribution CMI knowing that it has been removed or altered without that authority (§ 1202(b)(2)); and distributing, importing for distribution, or publicly performing works, copies of works, or phonorecords, knowing that CMI has been removed or altered without that authority (§ 1202(b)(3)). A single concluding clause applies to all three paragraphs and adds a second knowledge requirement: the actor must know, or — for civil remedies under § 1203 — have reasonable grounds to know, that the act “will induce, enable, facilitate, or conceal an infringement of any right under this title.” Subsection (b) thus states two distinct mental-state elements: the one attached to the prohibited act itself (intentional removal or alteration under (b)(1); knowledge that CMI was removed or altered under (b)(2) and (b)(3)), and the separate forward-looking one in the concluding clause.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]

It does not resolve what counts as authority “of the copyright owner or the law,” whether an automated process that discards metadata is an “intentional” removal, or whether CMI must have been removed from the same copy that is later distributed — questions on which published district court decisions have divided and which this document does not survey. This clause does not address § 1202(a) (false CMI), the definition in § 1202(c), or the limitations in § 1202(d) and (e), each described in a separate clause, and it does not state whether any handling of A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. falls within the subsection. WHAT THE STATUTE DEFINES AS “COPYRIGHT MANAGEMENT INFORMATION”
17 U.S.C. § 1202(c) defines “copyright management information” as any of eight listed categories of information “conveyed in connection with copies or phonorecords of a work or performances or displays of a work, including in digital form,” and expressly excludes from the term any personally identifying information about a user of a work or of a copy, phonorecord, performance, or display of a work. The listed categories are: the title and other information identifying the work, including the information set forth on a notice of copyright (§ 1202(c)(1)); the name of, and other identifying information about, the author (§ 1202(c)(2)); the name of, and other identifying information about, the copyright owner, including the information set forth in a notice of copyright (§ 1202(c)(3)); with an exception for public performances of works by radio and television broadcast stations, identifying information about a performer whose performance is fixed in a work other than an audiovisual work (§ 1202(c)(4)) and, for an audiovisual work, about a writer, performer, or director credited in it (§ 1202(c)(5)); terms and conditions for use of the work (§ 1202(c)(6)); identifying numbers or symbols referring to such information or links to such information (§ 1202(c)(7)); and such other information as the Register of Copyrights may prescribe by regulation, except that the Register may not require the provision of any information concerning the user of a copyrighted work (§ 1202(c)(8)).

NINTH CIRCUIT: SECTION 1202(B) REQUIRES AN AFFIRMATIVE SHOWING ABOUT FUTURE INFRINGEMENT
In Stevens v. Corelogic, Inc., 899 F.3d 666 (9th Cir. 2018), real estate photographers alleged that a multiple-listing-service software vendor's image-resizing software stripped EXIF and IPTC metadata from their photographs, in violation of 17 U.S.C. § 1202(b)(1) and (b)(3). The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the software vendor, holding that both paragraphs require the defendant to have the mental state described in subsection (b)'s concluding clause, and that the plaintiff must make an affirmative showing — the court gave a past “pattern of conduct” or “modus operandi” as examples — that the defendant was aware, or had reasonable grounds to be aware, of the probable future impact of its actions. The court reasoned that the generic assertion that removing CMI makes infringement harder to detect “identifies a general possibility that exists whenever CMI is removed” and would render the statutory clause superfluous. At the same time, the court stated that because the statute is written in the future tense, a plaintiff need not show that a specific infringement has already occurred; the plaintiff must instead provide evidence from which future infringement can be inferred to be likely, though not certain, as a result of the removal or alteration. On the record there, neither photographer had used the metadata to detect infringement, and the court concluded the vendor was not liable under § 1202(b).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Both provisions thus require the defendant to possess the mental state of knowing, or having a reasonable basis to know, that his actions "will induce, enable, facilitate, or conceal" infringement."
  — Stevens v. Corelogic, Inc., 899 F.3d 666, 673-675 (9th Cir. 2018) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9022953/stevens-v-corelogic-inc/)
  "Applying that concept here, we hold that a plaintiff bringing a Section 1202(b) claim must make an affirmative showing, such as by demonstrating a past "pattern of conduct" or "modus operandi", that the defendant was aware or had reasonable grounds to be aware of the probable future impact of its actions."
  — Stevens v. Corelogic, Inc., 899 F.3d 666, 673-675 (9th Cir. 2018) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9022953/stevens-v-corelogic-inc/)
  "Instead, the plaintiff must provide evidence from which one can infer that future infringement is likely, albeit not certain, to occur as a result of the removal or alteration of CMI."
  — Stevens v. Corelogic, Inc., 899 F.3d 666, 673-675 (9th Cir. 2018) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/9022953/stevens-v-corelogic-inc/)
  Known gap: Stevens is a Ninth Circuit decision, binding federal precedent in the circuit that includes California but not a national rule; other circuits and district courts have described the § 1202(b) knowledge requirement in their own terms, and this clause does not survey them. The decision construes § 1202(b) only and says nothing about the distinct intent element of § 1202(a). It also does not decide whether the software's automated stripping of metadata was an “intentional” removal, because the case was resolved on the concluding-clause mental state. The opinion quoted here is the amended opinion reported at 899 F.3d 666, which superseded the panel's earlier opinion at 893 F.3d 648; the quotations are taken from CourtListener's rendering of the reported opinion, which that site labels as derived from a scanned document and therefore capable of containing typographical errors. Because the Ninth Circuit's own PDF host (cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov) is unreachable from this environment (the egress proxy refuses the connection with a 403) and CourtListener's authenticated API endpoints require credentials that are not available here, the second, independent verification for these three quotations was performed by querying CourtListener's public search index for each quoted phrase restricted to this opinion's cluster id (cluster_id:9022953), each of which returned exactly one matching opinion; the opinion page itself was also retrieved twice under two different browser header sets, and the two extractions were character-identical. This clause does not state whether any handling of A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. would satisfy or fail the showing the court described.

SECTION 1203: WHO MAY SUE AND WHAT THE COURT MAY ORDER
17 U.S.C. § 1203(a) provides that any person injured by a violation of § 1201 or § 1202 may bring a civil action in an appropriate United States district court. Section 1203(b) lists the powers of the court in such an action: it may grant temporary and permanent injunctions on terms it deems reasonable to prevent or restrain a violation, but in no event may impose a prior restraint on speech or press protected by the First Amendment (§ 1203(b)(1)); it may order impounding of any device or product in the alleged violator's custody or control that the court has reasonable cause to believe was involved in a violation (§ 1203(b)(2)); it may award damages under § 1203(c) (§ 1203(b)(3)); it may in its discretion allow recovery of costs by or against any party other than the United States or an officer of the United States (§ 1203(b)(4)); it may in its discretion award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party (§ 1203(b)(5)); and it may, as part of a final judgment or decree finding a violation, order the remedial modification or destruction of any device or product involved in the violation that is in the violator's custody or control or has been impounded (§ 1203(b)(6)).

SECTION 1203(C): ELECTING ACTUAL DAMAGES OR STATUTORY DAMAGES
Under 17 U.S.C. § 1203(c)(1), a person committing a violation of § 1201 or § 1202 is liable for either actual damages and any additional profits of the violator, as provided in § 1203(c)(2), or statutory damages, as provided in § 1203(c)(3). Section 1203(c)(2) directs the court to award the complaining party the actual damages it suffered as a result of the violation, plus any profits of the violator attributable to the violation and not taken into account in computing actual damages, if the complaining party elects those damages at any time before final judgment is entered. Section 1203(c)(3) sets two different statutory-damages ranges: for each violation of § 1201, not less than $200 or more than $2,500 per act of circumvention, device, product, component, offer, or performance of service; and for each violation of § 1202, not less than $2,500 or more than $25,000. The election, like the election of actual damages, may be made at any time before final judgment is entered.

SECTION 1203(C)(4)-(5): REPEAT VIOLATIONS, INNOCENT VIOLATIONS, AND NONPROFIT REMISSION
Section 1203(c) contains three adjustments to the damages otherwise awarded. Under § 1203(c)(4), if the injured party sustains the burden of proving, and the court finds, that a person violated § 1201 or § 1202 within three years after a final judgment was entered against that person for another such violation, the court may increase the award up to triple the amount otherwise awarded, as the court considers just. Under § 1203(c)(5)(A), the court in its discretion may reduce or remit the total award where the violator sustains the burden of proving, and the court finds, that the violator was not aware and had no reason to believe its acts constituted a violation. Under § 1203(c)(5)(B)(ii), that reduction is mandatory rather than discretionary for a nonprofit library, archives, educational institution, or public broadcasting entity: the court “shall remit damages” where such an entity carries the same burden of proving it was not aware and had no reason to believe its acts constituted a violation. Section 1203(c)(5)(B)(i) gives “public broadcasting entity” the meaning it has under 17 U.S.C. § 118(f).

SECTION 1202(D)-(E): GOVERNMENT ACTIVITIES AND BROADCAST TRANSMISSION LIMITATIONS
Section 1202 contains two express limitations. Section 1202(d) states that the section does not prohibit any lawfully authorized investigative, protective, information security, or intelligence activity of an officer, agent, or employee of the United States, a State, or a political subdivision of a State, or of a person acting under contract with any of them, and defines “information security” for that subsection as activities carried out to identify and address the vulnerabilities of a government computer, computer system, or computer network. Section 1202(e) limits liability under subsection (b) for broadcast stations, cable systems, and their programming suppliers. For analog transmissions, § 1202(e)(1) removes liability where avoiding the violating activity is not technically feasible or would create an undue financial hardship on the person, and the person did not intend by the activity to induce, enable, facilitate, or conceal infringement. For digital transmissions, § 1202(e)(2) provides parallel protection tied to whether a voluntary consensus standard for placement of CMI has been set, again only where the activity is not intended to induce, enable, facilitate, or conceal infringement. Section 1202(e)(3) takes the definitions of “broadcast station” and “cable system” from sections 3 and 602 of the Communications Act of 1934.

SECTION 1204: CRIMINAL OFFENSES AND PENALTIES FOR WILLFUL COMMERCIAL VIOLATIONS
17 U.S.C. § 1204(a) makes a violation of § 1201 or § 1202 a federal crime, but only where the violation is committed “willfully and for purposes of commercial advantage or private financial gain.” The penalties are a fine of not more than $500,000 or imprisonment of not more than 5 years, or both, for a first offense, and a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or imprisonment of not more than 10 years, or both, for a subsequent offense. Section 1204(b) states that subsection (a) does not apply to a nonprofit library, archives, educational institution, or public broadcasting entity as defined under 17 U.S.C. § 118(f). Section 1204(c) sets a five-year statute of limitations, providing that no criminal proceeding may be brought under the section unless commenced within 5 years after the cause of action arose.

expectedJSON.body: In Stevens v. Corelogic, Inc., 899 F.3d 666 (9th Cir. 2018), real estate photographers alleged that a multiple-listing-service software vendor's image-resizing software stripped EXIF and IPTC metadata from their photographs, in violation of 17 U.S.C. § 1202(b)(1) and (b)(3). The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the software vendor, holding that both paragraphs require the defendant to have the mental state described in subsection (b)'s concluding clause, and that the plaintiff must make an affirmative showing — the court gave a past “pattern of conduct” or “modus operandi” as examples — that the defendant was aware, or had reasonable grounds to be aware, of the probable future impact of its actions. The court reasoned that the generic assertion that removing CMI makes infringement harder to detect “identifies a general possibility that exists whenever CMI is removed” and would render the statutory clause superfluous. At the same time, the court stated that because the statute is written in the future tense, a plaintiff need not show that a specific infringement has already occurred; the plaintiff must instead provide evidence from which future infringement can be inferred to be likely, though not certain, as a result of the removal or alteration. On the record there, neither photographer had used the metadata to detect infringement, and the court concluded the vendor was not liable under § 1202(b).

citations.quote: Both provisions thus require the defendant to possess the mental state of knowing, or having a reasonable basis to know, that his actions "will induce, enable, facilitate, or conceal" infringement.

Applying that concept here, we hold that a plaintiff bringing a Section 1202(b) claim must make an affirmative showing, such as by demonstrating a past "pattern of conduct" or "modus operandi", that the defendant was aware or had reasonable grounds to be aware of the probable future impact of its actions.
Instead, the plaintiff must provide evidence from which one can infer that future infringement is likely, albeit not certain, to occur as a result of the removal or alteration of CMI.

citations.quote: Any person who violates section 1201 or 1202 willfully and for purposes of commercial advantage or private financial gain— (1) shall be fined not more than $500,000 or imprisoned for not more than 5 years, or both, for the first offense; and (2) shall be fined not more than $1,000,000 or imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both, for any subsequent offense.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, five-year limitations period for criminal proceedings
citations.quote: No criminal proceeding shall be brought under this section unless such proceeding is commenced within 5 years after the cause of action arose.

expectedJSON.gap: Criminal proceedings under § 1204 are brought by the United States; the section creates no private right to initiate a prosecution, and the civil action in § 1203 is independent of it. The statute does not define “willfully” or “commercial advantage or private financial gain” for this section, and this clause does not summarize the case law construing those terms in the copyright context. This clause does not quote 17 U.S.C. § 118(f), which supplies the “public broadcasting entity” definition and was not separately retrieved for this document, and it takes no position on whether conduct involving A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. could be charged under this section.
